_comment: Source of truth for the careers surface. data/careers.json -> scripts/generate-careers.js -> dist/careers.html + dist/careers/<slug>/index.html. Validated at build time; malformed data fails the build. TITLING RULE (v2, 2026-08-06): every public title uses a standardised core noun plus an optional comma qualifier. LinkedIn parses prefix/core/suffix and standardises on the core, so a qualifier after the comma costs no reach and buys self-selection. Never mint a new head noun — a novel title is silently mapped to whatever the model thinks it resembles, and has no neighbours in the recommender's embedding space. Niche vocabulary belongs in the body, never the title. Internal names for these seats live in kanan-ops/hiring/Hire_Archetypes_for_Sourcing_v1.md.

roles.title: Founding CTO
roles.timeline: Four conversations over about six weeks, then a paid architecture review
roles.summary: Own the engine that turns written regulation into software a customs officer, an underwriter and a court could all check.
roles.description:
This is a co-founder role in substance: founder-level equity, founder-standard vesting, and shared risk. We are direct about that from the first conversation.

Kanan Labs builds the reasoning layer for cross-border trade. Every container that crosses a border is governed by a stack of rules no single person holds in their head — tariff lines, origin criteria, licensing conditions, each with a citation and an effective date, each changing without notice. We are building the system that holds them, reasons over them, and can always show its working.

The technical core is a compiler. It takes primary regulation, turns it into typed and versioned rules, signs them, and hands them to a product engine that produces evidence an exporter can put in front of an authority. Determinism matters more than cleverness here: an answer that cannot name its source, its version and its effective date is not an answer.

What this job entails. There is a constitution, an enforced type system, a working signing chain over one sealed slice and a green test suite. There is not yet a running product. Closing that gap is the job. For the first eighteen months you will be building, not managing — there is no team yet, and the work in front of you is code. Later you will hire and lead one.

You do not need to know anything about customs. Nobody arrives knowing this domain; the founder is a trade lawyer and supplies it. What you cannot learn on the job is the instinct that a rule which was true last year may not be true today, and that a system which cannot say "unclear" will eventually say something false with confidence.
responsibilities: Own the compiler end to end — typed primitives in, signed and versioned rule packs out.
Make determinism real. Identical inputs produce byte-identical output, or there is a written reason why not.
Build the signing and provenance chain so every output traces to the instrument it came from.
Own privacy and data residency architecture — currently unowned, and the highest-severity item on the list.
Choose and build the knowledge substrate, including how the system handles a rule that changes retroactively.
Set the engineering bar, then hire against it.
lookingFor: You have built and maintained production systems where being wrong was expensive.
Strong Python, and a preference for typed contracts over flexible dictionaries.
You have worked with versioned data or schemas that had to stay correct as the underlying rules changed.
You can explain why a fast non-deterministic answer can be worse than a slower deterministic one when the output has to be defended.
You are comfortable being the only engineer for a while.
niceToHave: Experience inside a standards-bound domain — healthcare terminology, financial reporting, tax, payments, identity — where the specification sat upstream of your opinion.
Knowledge representation, ontologies, rules engines, or formal methods.
Applied cryptography for evidence: signatures, canonicalisation, tamper-evident logs.
Compiler or interpreter design. Bitemporal or versioned data modelling.
Any exposure at all to customs, trade, tax or insurance regulation.

roles.title: Founding Engineer (Full-Stack)
roles.timeline: Two conversations, then a paid exercise — about three weeks end to end
roles.summary: Build the product around the engine: document intake, extraction, reconciliation, and the screen a reviewer signs their name to.
roles.description:
Kanan Labs builds software that tells an exporter whether their shipping documents will survive contact with a customs authority — before the container sails, not after the refund is stuck.

There is an engine that produces signed, checkable rules. There is nothing yet that puts one in front of a human being about to send a container to Rotterdam. You build that.

What this job entails. Concretely: the service layer that does not exist yet; document intake that copes with an invoice photographed at an angle; extraction where every field carries its source page and confidence rather than arriving as a bare string; reconciliation that can say exactly which of three documents disagrees and where; and the reviewer console the whole product is judged on. You will often be the person who writes the specification rather than the person who receives it.

You will not be alone in the sense that matters — the architecture is opinionated and already written down, and you consume it rather than redesign it. Arguing that it should change is welcome; there is a documented process for that.

You do not need customs experience and we do not expect it. What we do expect is that you have built something end to end that another person then depended on, and that you can talk about the parts of it that went wrong.
responsibilities: Build the API layer between the rules engine and everything downstream.
Build document intake and classification, where "we are not sure what this is" is a real answer rather than a crash.
Build the extraction pipeline so every extracted field carries its source, its page and its confidence.
Build cross-document reconciliation — invoice, packing list and bill of lading must agree, and the system must say where they do not.
Build the packet engines and the reviewer console.
Ship weekly, in front of real users, from early on.
lookingFor: Roughly two to six years building software other people relied on. Internships and your own projects count.
Python and TypeScript — or clear evidence you pick up a stack in a fortnight.
You have worked across the stack: an API, a database and a screen, all yours.
You are comfortable integrating vendor APIs rather than rebuilding them.
You write clearly. This company runs on written documents.
niceToHave: Document AI or OCR — Docling, Azure Document Intelligence, Surya, Marker, Unstructured, or similar.
Next.js, TypeScript in strict mode, Tailwind, shadcn.
PostgreSQL beyond CRUD — migrations, constraints, query plans.
You have worked somewhere the output had to be defended: finance, healthcare, legal, logistics.
A public trail of things you have built. A good repository beats a good CV here and we will read it.

roles.title: Head of Customs & Trade Compliance
roles.location: Bengaluru — with regular time in the Chennai–Hosur corridor
roles.timeline: One conversation, then a short paid project — about four weeks, part-time
roles.summary: The person who knows what actually happens at the customs hall, and makes the software agree with it.
roles.description:
Kanan Labs builds software that checks an exporter's shipping documents against the rules before the container sails. That claim is worth nothing unless somebody here has personally watched it fail at a port.

That is you. You are the reason our rules are right rather than merely well-formed, the person a customer talks to when a refund has not landed, and the person a prospective design partner believes within thirty seconds because you have obviously done the job.

What this job entails. Three things. You check every rule the system encodes against what actually happens — the person who says "that condition is correct on paper and wrong at the air cargo complex." You own delivery: reviewer workflow, what a packet must contain before a broker or an underwriter will accept it, onboarding, and the customer who writes in at 9pm. And you carry the conversations with exporters who might become our first design partners.

Two things we will say plainly rather than leave you to discover. First, this pays substantially more than the same work inside a broking firm, fully declared, with equity on top — we would rather state that than play a negotiation game. Second, and following from it, this is not a role where you keep a side practice. We will ask directly, because the entire product is an argument about defensibility and we cannot make that argument with a divided book.

This is not a sales role and there is no quota. It is also not a role for someone who has supervised the work without ever having done it.
responsibilities: Check encoded rules against operational reality, and be the internal authority when they disagree.
Own the delivery backbone — reviewer workflow, packet acceptance, onboarding, customer queries.
Define what a shipping-bill or marine-insurance packet must contain before a broker or underwriter will sign it.
Carry design-partner conversations with exporters, brokers and forwarders.
Sit with the engineers often enough that the product is shaped by the port, not by a diagram.
lookingFor: Eight years or more in customs clearance, export documentation or freight forwarding.
You have filed, or directly supervised the filing of, real shipping bills. Not managed a team that did — done it.
You can explain why an IGST refund gets stuck, and whose obligation the missing step usually was.
Tamil. This is a hard requirement — the corridor runs Chennai, Ranipet, Hosur, Krishnagiri and Coimbatore.
You want your income fully on the books.
niceToHave: G-card, or having sat and passed the Customs Brokers Licensing Regulation 6 examination.
You have chosen or rolled out software at a broking firm or forwarder, or implemented it from the vendor side — Logi-Sys, Trezix, Kale, Automaxis, ODeX or similar.
AEO application experience. Surviving a customs audit of your own internal controls is a strong signal.
EV components, auto ancillaries, or anything that has made you argue about Chapter 85.
Marine cargo insurance exposure, broker-side or claims-side.

roles.title: Trade Compliance Analyst (Regulatory Content)
roles.timeline: A conversation, a three-hour exercise on real regulatory text, then a session where we argue with your answers
roles.summary: Read primary regulation and turn it into rules a machine can run and an auditor can check.
roles.description:
Somebody has to read the Customs Act, the Foreign Trade Policy, the IRDAI broker regulations and a stack of notifications, and turn what they say into something software can evaluate without lying about it. That is this job.

If you have worked in regulatory content, statutory compliance libraries, indirect tax content, patent drafting or trade compliance at a manufacturer, you have done a version of this already — reading a primary instrument and producing a structured obligation with a trigger, a date and an evidence requirement. We are asking you to do it with more precision than anyone has asked before, and to stop paraphrasing.

What this job entails. You work from primary text, never a summary or a commentary. Each rule you produce carries the exact span it came from, the dates between which it applies, what evidence would satisfy it, and what it supersedes. When a provision genuinely cannot be resolved on the facts a system will ever hold, you say so and it becomes a state the software surfaces — not a footnote nobody reads. And you keep all of it correct through amendment cycles, which is the part that is invisible when it works.

You do not need to write code and we will not test you on it. You do need to be comfortable with structure: decision tables, if-then conditions, typed fields.

We are not filtering on the prestige of your degree, and we are not looking for policy writing. This is not a role about how trade ought to be regulated. It is a role about what the rule currently says, exactly, and what it would take to prove it.
responsibilities: Read primary instruments and produce structured, executable rules with span-level citation.
Get the dates right — when a rule took effect, when it stopped, and what replaced it.
Define evidence requirements: which document, issued by whom, bearing which field, would satisfy an auditor.
Flag genuinely unresolvable provisions rather than picking an interpretation.
Keep the rule base correct as notifications amend it, and know what changed and why.
lookingFor: Two to six years working with primary legal, regulatory, tax or standards text.
You work from the source. If your instinct on an unfamiliar provision is to find a good summary of it, this is the wrong role.
You are comfortable with structure — decision tables, conditions, schemas, typed fields.
You can recognise when a provision cannot be decided on the available facts, and say so.
You will hold a position under pressure from a founder who disagrees with you.
niceToHave: Regulatory or trade content work — compliance libraries, tax content, legal publishing, XBRL taxonomies, or a regtech content team.
Registered patent agent, or a law degree taken after an engineering or science degree.
Customs, DGFT, foreign trade policy, HSN classification, SCOMET or marine insurance regulation specifically.
Indirect tax or GST content, especially where you owned what happens when a notification lands mid-year.
Any exposure to rules-as-code, decision modelling or knowledge representation.

roles.title: Senior Data Engineer, Regulatory Data
roles.timeline: Two conversations, then a paid exercise on a problem we are currently stuck on
roles.summary: Build the pipelines that notice when the law changes, and turn that change into something the product can act on.
roles.description:
Indian trade regulation moves constantly. A duty remission rate is halved in February and restored in March. A notification supersedes another notification that amended a third. Nobody sends you an email about it, and an exporter finds out at the port.

You build the system that watches, diffs, extracts and routes — so a change in a circular becomes a machine-readable delta with an owner and a deadline, hours after it is published.

What this job entails. Ingestion across a long tail of government sources that were never designed to be parsed. Structural diffing that says "this clause changed, in this way, with effect from this date" rather than "this page changed." Extracting obligations from prose into something typed. Mapping an obligation to the specific customers it actually affects, so an alert is about them rather than about everyone. And temporal queries, because "what were the rules on the date of this shipment" is a different and much harder question than "what are the rules."

This is the asset that compounds. Products pivot; a versioned, diffed corpus of trade regulation survives all of it and is worth more every month.

One thing we will say plainly because it comes up: we are not looking for sentiment analysis. Regulation carries obligation, not opinion, and a sentiment score over a government circular is both noise and impossible to audit. The techniques that matter here are change detection, information extraction, entity resolution and temporal reasoning. If you want to argue with that, do — it would be a good conversation.

You do not need to know trade law. You do need to care that an extracted fact without a citation and a date is worse than no fact at all.
responsibilities: Build and run ingestion across government sources — notifications, circulars, tariff schedules, restricted-party lists.
Build structural diffing that identifies what changed at clause level, and from when.
Extract obligations from prose into typed records that carry their citation.
Map obligations to the customers they affect, using their commodity codes, ports and destinations.
Build temporal query support so the system can answer as of a past date.
Own data quality, because everything downstream inherits it.
lookingFor: Roughly three to seven years building data pipelines in production.
Strong Python and SQL, and comfort with the messy end: scrapers that break, PDFs that are images, ten different date formats.
You have done information extraction, change detection or entity resolution on real data, not in a notebook.
You treat provenance as a requirement rather than a nice-to-have.
You can run something that has to be right every day, not just once.
niceToHave: Regulatory, legal or government text specifically — horizon scanning, compliance content, legal publishing, or a regtech product team.
Document AI and layout-aware extraction.
Temporal or bitemporal data modelling; knowledge graphs.
Multilingual extraction.
You have worked somewhere the extraction had to be defended to an auditor.
